visuals.title: Where transfused iron settles
visuals.text: Transfusions bring iron faster than the body excretes it: haemosiderosis. Desferrioxamine chelates it.

glossary.Haemoglobin: The iron-containing protein in red cells that carries oxygen, made of four globin chains around haem.
glossary.Globin: The protein chains of haemoglobin; adults mostly have two alpha and two beta.
glossary.Beta-globin: One of the two chain types in adult haemoglobin; mutated in sickle cell and beta-thalassaemia.
glossary.Alpha-globin: The chain present in all normal haemoglobins; four genes code for it.
glossary.Homozygous: Having two identical faulty copies of a gene, one from each parent.
glossary.Heterozygous: Having one faulty and one normal copy of a gene; usually a carrier or mild form.
glossary.Anaemia: A low haemoglobin, reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.
glossary.Jaundice: Yellowing of skin and eyes from raised bilirubin, here from red cell breakdown.
glossary.Failure to thrive: A child not gaining weight or growing as expected.
glossary.Abdominal fullness: A swollen-feeling tummy, here from a big liver and spleen.
glossary.Ferritin: The iron-storage protein; normal in thalassaemia trait but low in iron deficiency.
glossary.Alpha-thalassaemia major: Loss of all four alpha-globin genes, so no normal fetal or adult haemoglobin can be made.
glossary.Gamma chains: The globin chains of fetal haemoglobin, which replace beta chains before birth.
glossary.Hydrops fetalis: Severe fluid build-up in a fetus from heart failure due to profound anaemia.
glossary.Vaso-occlusion: Blockage of small blood vessels, here by rigid sickle cells.
glossary.Intercurrent illness: Another illness, such as an infection, happening at the same time.
glossary.Henna: A plant dye for skin and hair; an oxidant that can trigger haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
glossary.Sulfa-drugs: Sulphonamide-containing drugs such as co-trimoxazole; oxidant triggers in G6PD deficiency.
glossary.Nitrofurantoin: An antibiotic for urinary infections; an oxidant trigger in G6PD deficiency.
glossary.Quinolones: Antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin; can trigger G6PD haemolysis.
glossary.Dapsone: An antibiotic used for leprosy and some skin diseases; a strong oxidant.
glossary.NSAIDs: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen.
glossary.Stroke: Brain damage from a blocked or burst blood vessel; a major sickle cell risk in children.
glossary.Splenic dysfunction: A spleen that no longer filters bacteria well, raising infection risk.
glossary.Iron overload: Too much iron stored in the body, damaging organs.
glossary.MCP joints: Metacarpophalangeal joints: the knuckles where fingers meet the hand.
glossary.Hyperpigmented skin: Darker skin, here from iron deposits.
glossary.Macules: Flat, coloured spots on the skin.
glossary.Gold standard: The most accurate test available for confirming a diagnosis.
glossary.FBC: Full blood count: haemoglobin, red cell indices, white cells and platelets.
glossary.Blood transfusion: Giving donated red cells into a vein.
glossary.IV fluids: Fluids given into a vein; in sickle crisis they help reduce sickling.
glossary.Prophylactic antibiotics: Regular antibiotics (often penicillin) to prevent infection in a poorly functioning spleen.
glossary.Vaccination: Immunisation, here against pneumococcus, meningococcus and influenza.
glossary.Point mutation: A change in a single DNA base.
glossary.Polymerise: Link together into long chains; deoxygenated HbS does this inside red cells.
glossary.Deoxygenated: Having given up its oxygen, as in tissues and small veins.
glossary.End-organ ischaemia: Organ damage from poor blood supply.
glossary.Precipitate: Come out of solution and clump inside the cell.
glossary.Unpaired chains: Excess alpha or beta chains with no partner, which clump and damage red cell precursors.
glossary.Erythropoiesis: Production of red blood cells in the bone marrow.
glossary.Bone marrow expansion: The marrow enlarging to make more red cells, thinning and reshaping the bones.
glossary.Skeletal deformity: Abnormally shaped bones, such as an enlarged forehead or cheekbones.
glossary.Pentose phosphate pathway: A side branch of glucose metabolism that makes NADPH; G6PD is its first enzyme.
glossary.Oxidative haemolysis: Red cell destruction caused by oxidant damage to haemoglobin and membranes.
glossary.Oxidant: A chemical that removes electrons and damages proteins and membranes.
glossary.Fetal haemoglobin: HbF: two alpha and two gamma chains; it does not sickle.
glossary.Excrete: Get rid of from the body; humans have no active way to excrete iron.
